_comment: Hindu expansion 175-drive N: Mahabharata later and framing episodes (Ganguli 1883-96; Harivamsha prose translation, public domain).

title.zh: 耶伐克里陀與太陽的戰爭

region.zh: 俱盧之野荒地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, Yavakrida episode

summary.en: The boy Yavakrida, watching a seer's son humiliate his father, vowed to outdo the sun: he stood in the river's stream with arms up, reciting the Vedas against the sunrise, determined to learn by power what discipline teaches by time. The Sun came down as an old brahmin and explained the fraud in one speech - knowledge is not a siege - and warned him twice. His warnings unheeded, the age collected: the boy died by another man's wife, in the way his own violence had chosen.
summary.zh: 目睹仙人之子羞辱其父的少年耶伐克里陀，誓要勝過太陽：立於河流之中高舉雙臂，向日出誦讀吠陀，要以力量奪取只有紀律才能教授之物。太陽化作老婆羅門降下，一席話說破其欺騙——知識非圍城可得——並警告他兩次。警告未被理會，因果到場：少年死於他人之妻，以他自己所選的暴力方式。

passages.text: The vow was a child's siege: he stood waist-deep in the river at dawn, arms raised, reciting scripture against the sun itself - learn by force what the fathers learned by patience.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Sun came down in an old man's shape and gave the lesson the boy would not buy: knowledge is a path, not a wall; water does not flow by being bullied - nor does wisdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The warning's fine print was about women: treat another's wife as fire's edge. The boy forgot it; the debt was called, and the epic's water-story ended in a well - the siege broken from inside.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

region.zh: 赴象城之路（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Udyoga/Adi Parva traditions, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Shalya episode

summary.en: The Madra king Shalya, marching to join the Pandavas, was met on the road by a host whose hospitality he could not refuse - food, shelter, gifts beyond measure. Only at the end was the host named: Duryodhana's agents had bought the uncle of Nakula and Sahadeva into the Kaurava army - and honor-bound by the feast, Shalya went to war against his own sister's sons, serving as Karna's charioteer and complaining the whole way.
summary.zh: 馬德羅王沙利耶率軍來投般度族，途中受一位主人無法拒絕的款待——食物、屋舍、無法計量的贈禮。直到最後主人才被指名：難敵的代理者用盛宴把無種與偕天的舅舅買進了俱盧軍——受恩諾所縛，沙利耶對妹妹的兒子們作戰，充當迦爾納的御者，且一路上抱怨不休。

passages.text: The road-host's welcome was engineered: a stranger's table beyond refusal, a night of comfort, gifts that weighed more than armies - and a guest does not ask his host's name before the feast is done.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The host's name, when it came, was the war itself: the uncle of the youngest Pandavas had eaten his way into the enemy's roster, courtesy as conscription.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: He kept the bargain and cursed it daily: as Karna's charioteer he praised the enemy's aim to the man holding the bow - the epic's comedy of honor, a general going to war against his own blood at a dinner's invitation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

title.zh: 穆周昆陀的沉睡與迦羅耶梵之灰

region.en: Cave in the western hills (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Harivamsha / Mahabharata traditions, 19th-c. English prose translation (public domain)

source.work: A Prose English Translation of Harivamsha, 19th c. (public domain), the story of Muchukunda

summary.en: The human king Muchukunda had fought the gods' wars and been promised a sleep no age could break - a nap worth an eternity. Ages later Krishna, pursued by the barbarian Kalayavana, led the pursuer into a dark cave where a shape lay sleeping; Kalayavana kicked it awake, and the sleep-warmed gaze of the old warrior burned him to ash at one look. Krishna was forgiven the trick with a king's blessing.
summary.zh: 凡人國王穆周昆陀曾為諸神作戰，被允諾一場無齡可破的沉睡——一場等值永恆的午睡。無數劫後，被蠻王迦羅耶梵追擊的克里希那將追兵引入一處黑暗洞窟，其中躺著一個沉睡的身影；迦羅耶梵踢醒它，老戰士睡暖的目光一眼將他燒為灰燼。克里希那以王者的祝福被饒恕此計。

passages.text: The pension of a soldier-king: after the gods' wars were won, Muchukunda asked only for rest - and was granted a sleep that would not end until he chose to wake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harivamsha traditions (19th-c. prose translation); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kalayavana, the age's other tyrant, chased Krishna into the hills and into the cave; the dark shape on the stone floor was kicked - and the first thing it saw burned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harivamsha traditions (19th-c. prose translation); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king's sleep-glare, hoarded through the ages, had become a weapon he did not know he owned; he blessed the god who had used it and went to the forest to think about what he had seen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harivamsha traditions (19th-c. prose translation); not verbatim.

title.en: Sahadeva Who Knew Everything and Said Nothing

texts.period: Mahabharata, epic traditions, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), epic traditions on Sahadeva

summary.en: The epic's tradition of the youngest Pandava: having eaten his father Pandu's brain (in the folk-telling of the twins), Sahadeva could see everything that would happen - the dice, the exile, the war, the deaths - on one condition: he must never tell anyone, or the knowledge would kill him. He spent the whole epic as the family's silent oracle, smiling at disasters he was forbidden to name.
summary.zh: 史詩對般度幼子的傳說：據民間講述，雙生子中偕天曾食其父般度之腦，因而能預見一切將至之事——骰局、流放、戰爭、死亡——但有一條件：永不可告訴任何人，否則此知將殺死他。他終其史詩生涯作為家族沉默的神諭，對自己被禁止言說的災難報以微笑。

sensitivity.note: Folk-epic tradition rather than critical-edition text; recorded as tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The folk-telling gives the knowledge a price: the father's essence eaten, the sight of all futures granted - on the single condition of total silence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of epic/folk traditions on Sahadeva (Ganguli 1883-96 and vernacular tradition); not verbatim.

passages.text: The silence is the tragedy's engine: he watched the dice game as an oracle watches a wreck he is forbidden to announce - his smile at catastrophe is the tradition's blackest joke.
passages.note: Paraphrase of epic/folk traditions on Sahadeva (Ganguli 1883-96 and vernacular tradition); not verbatim.

passages.text: The epic uses him as its own narrator's shadow: the story that knows its ending and cannot say so - which is, of course, what a written epic is.
passages.note: Paraphrase of epic/folk traditions on Sahadeva (Ganguli 1883-96 and vernacular tradition); not verbatim.

texts.period: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Sabha Parva, the maya-sabha

summary.en: In the Pandavas' hall of illusions, Duryodhana - touring his cousins' splendor in envy - stepped on water that looked like floor and fell into water that looked like floor. Draupadi laughed. The tradition treats that one laugh as the war's true fuse: the shame-burned prince demanded a rematch of pride, got it at the dice, and the thigh he later showed her in the assembly was the insult's revenge.
summary.zh: 在般度族的幻宮中，懷妒參觀表親華貴宮殿的難敵，踏上看似地板的水而跌入看似水的地板。黑公主笑了。傳統視那一笑為戰爭真正的導火索：恥辱燒灼的王子要求一場傲慢的重賽，得之於骰局，而他後來在廷上向她亮出的那條腿，正是羞辱的報復。

passages.text: The hall was Maya's masterpiece: floors that were water, water that was floor - a prince of the real world taking the tour like an audit, and losing the audit to architecture.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Draupadi's laugh was a queen's laughter at a rival's clumsiness - and the epic marks the sound as the point of no return: pride is the war's currency, and she had just devalued his.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The rematch was the dice; the revenge was the thigh in the assembly; and the tradition's ledger shows a kingdom traded for one second of laughter - the price, the epic insists, was always known to both sides.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mace Duel: Bhima and Duryodhana

texts.period: Mahabharata, Shalya Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Shalya Parva, the mace duel

summary.en: The war's last duel was two mace-men on empty ground: Bhima, the appetite, against Duryodhana, the grudge - fighting for hours on even terms while the whole war watched. Krishna touched his own thigh; Bhima understood, and below the waist - where the vow had been sworn in the dice-hall - the mace came down. The code was broken by a vow, and the winner was jeered by the loser to the end.
summary.zh: 戰爭的最後決鬥是空地上兩位杵士：怖軍，以食量為徽；難敵，以積怨為徽——在兩軍注視下於均勢中激戰數小時。克里希那拍了拍自己的大腿；怖軍會意，在腰以下——誓言於骰廳所立之處——鐵杵落下。規矩被一個誓言打破，而勝者至終仍被敗者譏笑。

passages.text: The duel was even: mace on mace, hour after hour, the war's two appetites - food and grudge - deciding the age's account in single combat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Shalya Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Krishna's hand on his own thigh was the hint the vow required: the dice-hall's oath - thy thigh - answered below the waist, where the code forbade and the promise demanded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Shalya Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The dying king's last speech refused the verdict: my brothers are dead, I broke no promise I kept - and the epic leaves the winner standing on a broken rule while the loser keeps his argument.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Shalya Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

region.zh: 鄔婆普拉婆耶，摩蹉都城（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Udyoga Parva, the muster

summary.en: The war was scheduled in a tent: the Pandavas, their exile ended, mustered allies at Upaplavya - and Krishna gave both sides the same arithmetic: I am one; choose me or my army. Duryodhana took the army and slept content; Arjuna took the unarmed god. The muster-scene is the epic's own calculus of force: numbers against alignment.
summary.zh: 戰爭在一頂帳中定下日程：流放期滿的般度五子於鄔婆普拉婆耶集合盟友——克里希那給予雙方同一道算術：我是一個人；選我或選我的軍隊。難敵取軍隊而酣然滿足；阿周那取空手之神。點兵之景是史詩自身的力量算術：數量對陣營之選。

passages.text: The tent was a stock exchange of oaths: kings pricing their loyalty, elephants and grain and spears - the epic pauses the story to show the war being priced.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Krishna's offer split the difference between gods and economics: one god, or a full akshauhini - and the tyrant chose what could be counted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Arjuna's choice - the charioteer, unarmed - is the epic's whole theology in one transaction: alignment outnumbers arithmetic, and the war proved it for eighteen days.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

region.zh: 般遮羅，祭地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, the fire-born pair

summary.en: Humiliated at Draupada's court and half-remembering a previous life, the seer Yaja was asked for a son to destroy Drupada. From the fire he built rose first a youth in armor - Dhrishtadyumna, whose destiny was written in the smoke - and then, at the seer's cry, a grown maiden, dark-eyed, beautiful, with a voice already carrying a sentence: 'I shall be the cause of the destruction of the Kauravas.' Draupadi's first words were a war plan.
summary.zh: 受辱於德魯帕陀王廷且半記前生的仙人耶耶被請求賜一個毀滅德魯帕陀之子。自其所築之火中先升起一位披甲青年——德羅什塔底優那，其命運已書於煙中——繼而於仙人呼喊之際，一位成年少女立於火中：黑眸、美麗，聲音中已攜一個句子：『我將成為俱盧族毀滅之因。』黑公主的第一句話即作戰計劃。

passages.text: The rite was aimed at a king's humiliation; the fire answered with personnel: first the armored son, tall as a standard, then the seer called for a daughter too - and the smoke made one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: She stepped from the flames grown, perfumed as a bride, and announced her purpose to the assembly like a commander briefing a war.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fire-born woman kept her sentence for twenty years and then executed it: her swayamvara, her laughter, her disrobing - the whole fuse of Kurukshetra was manufactured at one hearth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
